title: germanys power growth could reignite industrial engine 2026 06 10
author: Gavin Maguire
text:
LITTLETON, Colorado, June 10 (Reuters) - Germany's electricity output is on track to expand by the most in more than a decade in 2026, offering a potential lifeline to the industrial sector at the heart of Europe's biggest economy after years of near-stagnation.
Total utility-supplied electricity output from January through May has expanded ​by the most in more than a decade, to 209 terawatt hours (TWh), according to energy think tank Ember.
That surge in power output has coincided with tentative signs of stabilisation in ‌parts of the country's manufacturing sector, including some energy-intensive industries
, opens new tab
 such as chemicals.
To be sure, total activity and output levels across Germany's critical industrial base remain well below previous peaks, and total utility-supplied electricity output remains around 19% below the all-time peak set in 2017.
But thanks to rapid expansions in combined output from solar and wind farms - up 15% year-to-date and by 72% since 2017 - Germany's clean power supplies are approaching multi-year highs and look set to deliver the strongest annual growth in total electricity supply ​in several years.
That shift matters because energy availability and affordability have been a major binding constraint on German industry since the 2022 energy crisis triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Several major ​European energy importers cut purchases of Russian oil and gas in response, sharply tightening local energy markets.
The resulting surge in fuel and power costs hammered margins for German ⁠businesses, forced output cuts, and triggered a broader contraction across energy-intensive sectors that underpin the country's manufacturing model.
Now, the reverse dynamic may be starting to take hold.
As wind and solar output climb, they are injecting ​large volumes of low-cost electricity into the grid, helping to cap wholesale prices and improve supply stability.
Wholesale spot power prices in Germany so far in 2026 have averaged around 96.4 euros per megawatt hour, broadly flat ​compared with a year earlier and the lowest for the period in two years.
For industrial users, even a modest easing in power costs can have an outsized impact on profitability and production decisions.
Early signs suggest that some easing may be feeding through. Producers of chemicals and other energy-intensive goods, among the hardest hit in recent years, are showing tentative signs of stabilisation alongside the rise in available power supply.
The key difference this time is the source of the expansion.
Germany ​is not relying on fossil fuels or imports to boost supply, but on domestically generated renewables. Wind remains the backbone of the system, while solar is rapidly emerging as a major contributor, repeatedly setting new output ​records.
That matters for two reasons. First, renewable generation comes with near-zero marginal costs, which means that increases in output tend to push down overall power prices over time.
Second, domestically generated electricity reduces exposure to volatile global fuel markets, improving ‌supply security and ⁠predictability for industrial users.
Together, those dynamics create a more favourable operating environment for manufacturers than at any point since before the energy crisis.
None of this guarantees a full industrial revival.
German manufacturing is still grappling with weak global demand, rising competition from abroad, and structural changes in key sectors such as autos and chemicals.
Output across much of the industrial base remains below pre-pandemic levels, and any recovery is likely to be gradual.
There are also constraints within the power system itself. Grid bottlenecks, intermittency from renewables, and the need for expanded storage capacity could all limit how quickly rising generation translates into consistently lower prices.
And while electricity output is ​rising, total demand has yet to fully recover, reflecting ​the still-cautious stance of industrial users.
Still, the direction of travel is becoming clearer.
Germany's industrial sector does not need a return to ultra-cheap energy to stabilise — it needs predictability, scale and gradual cost relief.
The expansion in electricity supply is beginning to deliver exactly that.
More available power could support higher industrial output, which in turn lifts electricity demand, encouraging further investment ​in generation capacity.
Over time, that feedback loop could help rebuild both the scale and competitiveness of Germany's industrial base.
Germany's economic fortunes have ​long been tied to the ⁠strength of its factories.
But after the energy shock broke that link, the path to recovery may be running in the opposite direction.
If the current surge in electricity supply continues, it won't just light homes or charge vehicles — it will quietly reset the economics of making things in one of the world's leading manufacturing hubs.
In that sense, the next chapter of Germany's industrial story may not begin on the factory floor, but on the grid.
(The opinions expressed ⁠here are those ​of the author, a columnist for Reuters.)
